chunks: "The memory hierarchy is a stack of storage levels where each level is bigger, slower and cheaper per bit than the one above it: registers, then L1, L2 and L3 cache, then main memory, which is DRAM, then storage like an SSD or disk.
The reason is that no single memory technology is fast, big and cheap at once.
The hierarchy fakes it by exploiting locality: programs reuse recent data and touch nearby data, so a small fast memory can hold the working set and satisfy most accesses.
Registers sit inside the core, hold a few dozen values, and are accessed in under a cycle. L1 cache is tens of kilobytes of SRAM at about 1 nanoseconds.
L2 and L3 get bigger, up to tens of megabytes, at maybe 4 to 15 nanoseconds. DRAM is gigabytes at 50 to 100 nanoseconds.
SSDs are hundreds of gigabytes at tens of microseconds, and spinning disks are milliseconds. What's stored: registers hold the operands being computed on right now.
Caches hold copies of recently used instructions and data. DRAM holds the running programs and their data. Storage holds everything persistently.
And you can quantify it: if L1 hits 95 percent at 1 nanoseconds and the rest goes through to 80 nanoseconds DRAM, average access time is 5 nanoseconds instead of 80."
